repos.title: MagicAnimate: Temporally Consistent Human Image Animation using Diffusion Model
repos.paper_summary: MagicAnimate is a diffusion-based framework for generating temporally consistent human image animation from a reference image and a DensePose motion sequence. The method inflates a 2D UNet into a 3D temporal UNet by inserting temporal attention layers to model cross-frame consistency. It replaces CLIP-based appearance conditioning with a trainable appearance encoder that extracts dense features from the reference image; these features are injected into the spatial self-attention layers via concatenation rather than residual addition. For long videos, the model processes overlapping segments and averages predictions in the overlap regions to smooth transitions. Training uses an image-video joint strategy to utilize diverse single-frame data. On the TikTok dataset, MagicAnimate reduces FVD to 179.07 and FID-VID to 21.75, outperforming the strongest baseline, DisCo, by 38.8% on FVD and 63.7% on FID-VID. On TED-talks, it achieves an FVD of 131.51 and FID-VID of 19.00. A stated limitation is higher L1 error on TED-talks due to the lack of background information in DensePose signals, though foreground L1 error remains comparable to baselines.

repos.title: AutoGluon-Tabular: Robust and Accurate AutoML for Structured Data
repos.paper_summary:
AutoGluon-Tabular is an open-source Python library that trains machine learning models on raw tabular data using a single API call. It improves accuracy by ensembling multiple model types—including LightGBM, CatBoost, Random Forests, and a custom neural network—via multi-layer stacking and repeated $k$-fold bagging. Unlike frameworks focused solely on hyperparameter optimization, AutoGluon automatically preprocesses heterogeneous data, including text and date columns, to handle missing values and unseen categories.

In experiments on 39 OpenML datasets and 11 Kaggle competitions with a 4-hour time limit, AutoGluon achieved an average rank of 1.84 among six evaluated frameworks. It outperformed all competitors on 23 of the 39 OpenML tasks and 7 of the 11 Kaggle tasks. On two Kaggle competitions, it surpassed 99% of participating teams after 4 hours of training. Ablation studies show that removing multi-layer stacking or the neural network component significantly degrades performance. The framework requires significant compute resources for optimal results and assumes data is stored in a single table without temporal dependencies.

repos.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
repos.paper_summary:
This paper presents a method for high-quality image synthesis using diffusion probabilistic models. The authors demonstrate that training on a weighted variational bound, derived from an equivalence to denoising score matching, yields superior sample quality compared to standard likelihood-based objectives.

The model learns to reverse a Markov chain that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data. By parameterizing the reverse process mean as a function that predicts the added noise $\epsilon$, the training objective simplifies to minimizing the expected squared error between true and predicted noise:

$$
L_{\mathrm{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \epsilon} \left[ \| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon, t) \|^2 \right]
$$

where $t$ is the time step, $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the data, and $\epsilon$ is standard Gaussian noise. Sampling proceeds by iteratively removing noise using this learned predictor. On unconditional CIFAR10, the model achieves an Inception score of 9.46 and a FID score of 3.17, outperforming previous unconditional baselines like SNGAN-DDLS (FID 15.4). On 256x256 LSUN datasets, it produces samples with FID scores of 7.89 for churches and 4.90 for bedrooms. A limitation noted in the analysis is that while sample quality is high, the lossless codelengths are not competitive with other likelihood-based models, as most bits describe imperceptible details.

repos.title: Grounding DINO: Marrying DINO with Grounded Pre-Training for Open-Set Object Detection
repos.paper_summary:
Grounding DINO is an open-set object detector that extends the DINO Transformer-based architecture with language inputs to detect arbitrary objects specified by category names or referring expressions. The model integrates a feature enhancer, language-guided query selection, and a cross-modality decoder to fuse vision and text modalities at three distinct stages: the neck, query initialization, and head. It employs a sub-sentence level text representation using attention masks to prevent interaction between unrelated category names during training.

Pre-trained on large-scale datasets including COCO, OpenImages, GoldG, and caption data, Grounding DINO achieves 52.5 AP on the COCO zero-shot detection benchmark without using any COCO training images. It sets a new record on the ODinW zero-shot benchmark with a mean 26.1 AP. On RefCOCO/+/g, it reaches 90.56% accuracy after fine-tuning. Limitations include inferior performance on rare LVIS categories compared to DetCLIPv2 and the generation of false positives in some cases.

repos.title: Distributed Inference and Fine-tuning of Large Language Models Over The Internet
repos.paper_summary: Petals is a decentralized system for inference and fine-tuning of large language models over the Internet. It uses pipeline parallelism, where servers hold consecutive transformer blocks and clients manage routing and attention caches. A fault-tolerant algorithm recovers from server failures by restoring state from client-side caches, while a load-balancing protocol assigns blocks to maximize throughput. The system supports parameter-efficient fine-tuning by keeping trainable weights on the client. Experiments on Llama 2 (70B) and BLOOM (176B) show that distributed inference is at least 10 times faster than local RAM offloading. For example, sequential inference on three T4 GPUs achieves 2.29 steps per second at 1 Gbit/s bandwidth, compared to 0.139 steps per second for offloading. In a real-world setup spanning Europe and North America with heterogeneous consumer GPUs, the system maintains functionality despite high latency and NAT traversal. Limitations include privacy concerns regarding data processed by external peers and performance degradation when network latency exceeds 100 ms.

repos.title: UFO: A UI-Focused Agent for Windows OS Interaction
repos.paper_summary:
UFO is a UI-focused agent for Windows that uses GPT-Vision to execute natural language requests across desktop applications. The system employs a dual-agent framework: a HostAgent selects the target application and creates a global plan, while an AppAgent iteratively executes specific actions on UI controls. A Control Interaction module grounds these decisions using `pywinauto` and the Windows UI Automation API to perform operations like clicking buttons or setting text. UFO supports cross-application tasks by switching contexts and storing execution results in shared memory.

The authors evaluate UFO on WindowsBench, a custom benchmark of 50 tasks spanning nine applications including Outlook, Word, and Edge. UFO achieves an 86% success rate and 89.6% completion rate, outperforming GPT-4 (42% success) and GPT-3.5 (24% success) baselines, which rely on human surrogates for action execution. UFO also completes tasks in fewer steps (5.48 average) than the baselines. Limitations include restricted support for applications not fully compatible with Windows UI Automation, such as Adobe Acrobat, and potential delays when navigating unfamiliar interfaces.

repos.title: InternVL: Scaling up Vision Foundation Models and Aligning for Generic Visual-Linguistic Tasks
repos.paper_summary:
**This document outlines the LaTeX guidelines for author responses in arXiv submissions, emphasizing structure, formatting, and clarity.**
- Addresses *rebuttal* limits: one-page PDFs allowed to address reviewers' comments without adding new contributions.
- Enforces a *two-column layout*: dimensions of 6.875 inches wide by 8.875 inches high for text areas, ensuring readability.
- Highlights *equation numbering importance*: necessary for clear reference, avoiding overlaps with main paper.
- Provides guidance on *figure inclusion*: centers graphics, advises on font sizing and line widths for clarity in printed copies.
- Maintains *anonymity rules*: prohibiting personal identifiers and external links in the response to ensure blind review integrity.

repos.title: OpenRLHF: An Easy-to-use, Scalable and High-performance RLHF Framework
repos.paper_summary: OpenRLHF is an open-source framework that distributes the four models required for PPO-based RLHF across separate GPUs to enable training of language models larger than 70 billion parameters. It uses Ray to schedule model placement, vLLM with tensor parallelism to accelerate sample generation, and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 for training updates. Weights are synchronized between the ZeRO and vLLM engines using NCCL. On LLaMA2 models trained on NVIDIA A800 GPUs, OpenRLHF completes one PPO epoch over 1024 prompts in 471 s for a 7B model and 4489 s for a 70B model, achieving speedups of 1.82x to 2.5x over an optimized DeepSpeed-Chat baseline. On AlpacaEval, the resulting 7B PPO model achieves a 63.5% win rate against its SFT counterpart, compared to 60.1% for DPO. The benchmark evaluates throughput only; it does not compare final alignment quality against other frameworks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RLHF and RLVR training is dominated by inference cost, and existing frameworks are hard for newcomers to adopt.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior frameworks force a choice between high performance and ease of use.

digest_headlines.heading: Design of OpenRLHF
digest_headlines.headline: OpenRLHF assigns GPUs to rollout and training roles under Ray, with vLLM generating responses.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OpenRLHF trains 1.22× to 1.68× faster than verl across three model sizes in Table 1.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations include no multimodal support, possibly lower peak performance than industrial frameworks, and upstream dependency risk.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion summarizes four design innovations and cites institutional adoption as validation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists contributors, adopting institutions, and the four-stage PPO workflow with its loss functions.

repos.title: E-Branchformer: Branchformer with Enhanced merging for speech recognition
repos.paper_summary:
E-Branchformer is an acoustic encoder for automatic speech recognition that modifies the Branchformer architecture by adding a depth-wise convolution to its merge module and stacking additional point-wise feed-forward networks. In Branchformer, self-attention and convolutional branches process input in parallel; their outputs are concatenated and projected linearly. E-Branchformer inserts a depth-wise convolution between the concatenation and the projection, allowing the model to exchange spatial information across adjacent time steps during the merge. The paper also interleaves macaron-style FFNs with the E-Branchformer blocks to increase capacity without significantly increasing parameter count.

Experiments use the attention-based encoder-decoder framework on LibriSpeech (approx. 1000 hours). With a Large model (148.9M parameters) and external language model shallow fusion, E-Branchformer achieves word error rates of 1.85% on test-clean and 3.71% on test-other. Adding Internal Language Model Estimation improves these to 1.81% and 3.65%, respectively, outperforming Conformer-AED baselines (1.84% / 3.95%) and Branchformer-AED (1.93% / 4.00%). Ablations show that kernel size 31 for the merge convolution yields the best performance compared to sizes 3, 15, or 63. Limitations include reliance on an external language model for the best results and evaluation restricted to the LibriSpeech dataset.

repos.title: RF-DETR: Neural Architecture Search for Real-Time Detection Transformers
repos.paper_summary: RF-DETR is a specialist detection transformer that uses weight-sharing neural architecture search to discover accuracy-latency Pareto curves for target datasets without re-training. The model replaces the LW-DETR backbone with DINOv2 and applies a scheduler-free training procedure. During training, it samples random configurations of image resolution, patch size, windowed attention blocks, decoder layers, and query tokens. At inference, grid search selects specific sub-nets from this single trained model to match hardware constraints. On COCO, RF-DETR (nano) achieves 48.0 AP at 2.3 ms latency, outperforming D-FINE (nano) by 5.3 AP. The 2x-large variant reaches 60.1 AP on COCO, the first real-time detector to exceed 60 AP. On Roboflow100-VL, RF-DETR (2x-large) surpasses GroundingDINO (tiny) by 1.2 AP while running 20 times faster. The paper notes that latency measurements are sensitive to GPU power throttling, proposing a standardized buffering protocol for reproducible benchmarking.
